goals: Distinguish a population from a sample
State the Central Limit Theorem in plain English
Compute the standard error of a mean
why: The CLT is why polls of 1,000 people can describe a nation, and why A/B tests, quality control and confidence intervals work at all.
explain: The **population** is everyone you care about; a **sample** is the subset you actually measure. Sample statistics (like the sample mean) vary from sample to sample.

**Central Limit Theorem**: take many samples of size n and compute each sample's mean. Those means form a **normal** distribution, centred on the true mean, **whatever the shape of the original data**, as long as n is reasonably large (often 30+).
The spread of those sample means is the **standard error** (SE) = σ / √n. Quadrupling the sample size halves the uncertainty.
That is why averages are far more predictable than individual values: one customer's spend is wild; the average of 1,000 customers' spends is very stable.

formula.plain: Sample means are roughly normal around the true mean, with spread σ / √n.

example.title: Average basket size
steps: Individual baskets are skewed: mean ₹500, SD ₹300
So about 95% of sample means fall within ₹500 ± 2×30 = ₹440–₹560
example.result: You need 4× the data for 2× the precision, a key rule for budgeting surveys and experiments.

mistakes: Thinking the CLT makes the raw data normal. It is about the distribution of means.
Ignoring biased sampling: the CLT cannot fix a non-representative sample.

practice.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pop = rng.exponential(500, 1_000_000)          # very skewed "basket sizes"
means = [rng.choice(pop, 100).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
print(round(np.mean(means)), round(np.std(means), 1), round(pop.std() / 10, 1))  # SE ≈ σ/√n
